headline: High: LangGraph’s writable, networked orchestration can amplify unsafe outputs into shared state and external actions; the open-source list itself is inert.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is an inert awesome-list with no runnable surface, no I/O, and no shared channel. Profile B is a library-only orchestrator with developer-wired tools, but nothing in either profile shows A’s content being ingested by B by default. The pairwise prompt-injection pathway is therefore not evidenced.
conditions: IF a developer wires Profile A’s repository content into Profile B’s prompt or tool inputs, injection risk becomes relevant.
IF Profile B is configured to parse untrusted text from shared files or stdin as instructions, the pathway opens.
mitigations: Keep Profile A as a read-only reference source.
Do not feed raw repository text into Profile B prompts.
Add an instruction/content delimiter in any shared prompt template.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all B inputs.
requires-engineering: add a sanitizer that strips executable-looking directives from untrusted text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Profile A touches no data classes and has no egress. Profile B can read/write application-defined files and has broad network egress, but the only documented sensitive class is model provider API keys. Without a shared workspace or sensitive data in A, leakage is limited and not evidenced as a default pairwise flow.
conditions: IF Profile B is given a shared workspace containing secrets or regulated data, leakage risk increases.
IF Profile B logs or forwards application-defined files to model providers, data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of any shared directory.
Restrict Profile B to a dedicated workspace.
Disable or redact file-content logging in B.
Review which files B sends to model providers.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file allowlists for B egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Profile A has no write or execution capability, so it cannot contend for mutable state. Profile B can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem, while its concurrency model shares state via a checkpointer store. If A is later wrapped with writable tools, conflicts could emerge, but the documented pair itself is one-sided, so medium is the higher defensible severity under uncertainty.
conditions: IF Profile A is wrapped with write-capable tools against the same directory as B, write conflicts become possible.
IF multiple B instances share the same checkpointer store without locking, state races can occur.
mitigations: Separate A and B into different directories.
Avoid concurrent writes to the same checkpointer namespace.
Run B with a single writer during critical updates.
Check whether any shared state backend has locking enabled.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared state writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Profile A can publish curated content, and Profile B is a stateful orchestrator that can act on developer-defined tools and persistent graph state. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so medium fits better than low under the rubric’s uncertainty rule.
conditions: IF Profile B consumes Profile A’s output without verification, cascading errors can propagate.
IF B’s downstream tools perform external actions based on A-derived facts, impact increases.
mitigations: Require a verification step before B acts on A’s output.
Mark A’s content as advisory, not authoritative.
Add source citations to any A-derived claims.
Limit B’s downstream tools to dry-run mode first.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating before tool execution.

E_compliance.rationale: No regulated data class is documented for Profile A, and Profile B only explicitly handles model provider API keys plus application-defined graph state. There is no evidence of residency, certification, or retention mismatch in the pair, so compliance risk is limited to documented gaps rather than a concrete breach pathway.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into B’s graph state, compliance review is required.
IF deployment policy requires specific residency or retention guarantees, verify B’s backend satisfies them.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Document retention for B’s checkpointer store.
Confirm where B’s backend stores graph state.
Review whether any secrets are persisted.
requires-engineering: add policy checks for residency and retention.
